From Memex to Jelly

A connected history of how people reshape their software

Research reader · 1945 to 19 November 2026

A person can link two papers, write a rule in a spreadsheet, or ask an assistant to reshape a workspace. All three are acts of authorship. They give the person very different powers once someone else owns the software.

A question to take back to the lab

Imagine that you are preparing for a meeting with your professor. One paper is a PDF, your notes are in another app, a deadline is in your calendar, and a useful demonstration is paused in a browser tab. You want something quite modest: next to each claim in your notes, show the paper or demonstration that supports it, and tell me which claims I have not checked. You already possess the information. Why does making this little tool still feel like starting a software company?

That question has had several different answers. One generation gave people a way to link records. Another let people write rules inside the documents they were already using. Another tried to make independent tools work on the same material. Today a language model can propose a tool from a sentence. Each answer removes a different obstacle. None by itself answers the question a university should ask before adopting the result: who can change it, whose material can it use, and what happens to the change tomorrow?

Your library analogy captures the frustration. Here is the historically stronger version to say aloud: The Web helped independently maintained documents refer to one another. The next problem is that parts of one task live in independently maintained applications. Can we give the person doing the task a way to bring the relevant pieces together and change how they work? The Internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is one system that uses it; a browser is a program for accessing that system. A search engine is still another thing. No single person invented one application that suddenly collected all the world’s documents. Nor does bringing a map into a travel note require granting the map your whole notebook. N10 N11 R35

How to read this history. Read the chapter openings straight through for the story. Stop at the cases that answer your question; click the small reference codes to see the evidence. The dates are milestones, not a claim that research stopped between them. The source trails at the end cover all 75 bibliography positions in the public Jelly paper, the Ink & Switch essay’s linked readings and examples, and the public references from our earlier discussions. A connection described as a comparison is ours; a source appearing in another author’s bibliography is a documented citation, not proof that the second system descends directly from the first.

Four changes that sound like one change

You say What actually changes Who already made the decision?
“Write bananas: 3.” The content of one note. The developer already supplied typing.
“Put my timer on the left.” A setting, if that option exists. The developer supplied the choice; you select it.
“Whenever I write a banana quantity, total it.” A reusable rule that reacts to future edits. You specify the relationship. The system supplies a way to express it.
“Let my research group install this rule but keep each person’s note private.” The distribution of a feature and its authority. Someone must design the boundary; someone else must be able to inspect and enforce it.

The third row is the first place your notepad becomes interesting as a small piece of software. The fourth is where the question of differential agency becomes unavoidable. Notice that neither row says anything about the size of an AI model.

1945 to 1968 From finding a page to changing a relationship

1945 Vannevar Bush wanted to save a path through the evidence

Picture a researcher finishing a long search in a library. She found the two passages that make her argument work. Tomorrow another person can fetch the same volumes, but will they know why those two pages belong together? Bush’s problem in As We May Think was partly the growing scientific record, partly the mismatch between a formal index and the connections a reader actually makes. Looking up the correct heading and preserving a train of thought are different jobs. R01

His proposal was the Memex: a personal desk with viewing surfaces, controls and a store of material on microfilm. Microfilm is ordinary printed material photographed very small. A reader could bring items into view, add a note, and associate items into a trail that could be followed again. Imagine displaying a page about bows on one side and a note about materials on the other. The interesting action is linking the two. The screens belong to one imagined workstation; they are not two independent computers exchanging messages. The pictured desk was a concept, not a consumer machine that people purchased in 1945. R01

Here is the connection to your project, and also its limit. You can arrange sources in a way the original authors never planned. You have gained control over the relationship among records. You have not gained the ability to rewrite the desk’s functions. If a professor asks whether Memex was already malleable software, say: “It is an ancestor of the question. The user made the trail, but did not program a new kind of trail.”

1948 to 1960 The machine that waits for a person

1945 is our starting point, not the birthday of computing. Britain’s Manchester Baby ran a stored program in 1948; Cambridge’s EDSAC began running programs in 1949. A stored program is a set of instructions kept in memory. This let a machine change jobs by loading different instructions. That fact did not put a computer in every home, or make the instructions easy to change. The ability of a machine to be reprogrammed and the ability of an ordinary person to reprogram it are not the same achievement. N01 N02

In 1960 J. C. R. Licklider proposed a working partnership between people and computers. Think of the difference between submitting a final calculation to be run later and changing an assumption while looking at the result. In the second case, seeing the result can change the question. This was a research vision, not a product. It gives us a useful test for later inventions: is the computer simply finishing a job we already formulated, or helping us discover what job to do? N03

1962 and 1968 Douglas Engelbart built the working desk

At Stanford Research Institute, Douglas Engelbart asked how people working on hard problems could improve their collective ability to think. His 1962 report treated tools, language and working methods as parts of the same system. If you give someone a faster way to type but make it difficult for two people to revise an argument together, you have improved typing more than thinking. R02

What did the group actually make? NLS, an interactive computer system. In its 1968 demonstration an operator sat at a workstation with a display, keyboard, pointing device and keyset. The workstation connected to a larger computing system. In the demonstration material you can watch text being organized into an outline, links being followed and colleagues working across a distance. The mouse mattered because a person could point to something on the screen and act on it; NLS was much more than a mouse prototype. It was running research software, not a small home computer for sale. R04

Try the action with a piece of paper. Write “prepare talk,” and beneath it list “read Kay,” “check Jelly” and “make example.” Moving the whole branch keeps its children together. That is already a more powerful operation than moving marks on a page: the machine knows that these lines have a relationship. Bush imagined recording associations. Engelbart’s group built a working environment in which people could revise structured information together.

1963 and 1965 Two parallel ideas about structure

While Engelbart’s project was developing, Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad on the TX-2 research computer. A person used a light pen pointed at the display to draw and select objects. The system stored relationships, including geometric constraints. Draw two lines and require them to remain parallel: when you move one, the computer has something more meaningful to maintain than a collection of illuminated dots. Draw a reusable master symbol and place instances of it in a drawing. Editing the definition can affect the instances. This was working software described in a 1963 dissertation. R03

The useful comparison is a rectangle you drew by hand versus one you declared to have four right angles. Both may look identical until you drag a corner. Only the second has a rule that survives the edit. Whenever a modern prototype promises to preserve your intentions across a change, ask what its equivalent of “four right angles” is. A screenshot alone cannot tell you.

Theodor Nelson’s 1965 paper explored a file structure for writing and material that change and interconnect. Think of revising an argument without forcing every reader down one fixed sequence. Later, his account of transclusion described including material by reference. A copied paragraph and an embedded reference can look the same today; only the reference keeps a continuing connection to its source. Compare that with embedding a map view of a venue rather than pasting a screenshot of it. The systems are not identical; the distinction between copying and referring is the bridge. N04 J42

1972 to 1988 A computer you can author with

Dynabook was a design and Smalltalk was a working environment

Alan Kay’s 1972 Dynabook proposal asked what children and adults could do with a personal, portable computer as a medium for learning. “Medium” here means a material for expression. Paper accepts a story or a drawing; this proposed medium could also carry a simulation that responds. It was not a retail laptop. At Xerox PARC, Kay, Adele Goldberg, Dan Ingalls and colleagues worked on Smalltalk, a language and live programming environment. Kay and Goldberg’s 1977 paper describes working experiences on interim machines. It was not a 1977 Macintosh app that a student could download. R05 R07 N06

Think of a ball moving across the screen. A drawing program lets you paint the ball red. A simulation lets you change what happens when it reaches the floor. Double the energy lost on each bounce and the same ball settles sooner. You have changed a rule of the world, not just the picture. This is an explanatory example. In Smalltalk, objects respond to messages; a programmer can inspect and alter the behavior attached to objects in the live environment. “Live” means the result can be explored in the working system rather than merely described in a separate document. R07 N06 J24

This is why labels are dangerous in your presentation. Kay did not make Potluck or HyperCard. His contribution in this story is a question about the computer as a changeable medium, and participation in a team that built a powerful example. His 1984 article Computer Software and his separate piece on opening a word processor returned to how the material underneath a tool can be understood and altered. Ink & Switch points back to Kay; that supports a connection, not a claim to know the first person ever to use the word “malleable.” R09 N08 R43

1975 to 1979 Show the computer a procedure or give it a relationship

David Canfield Smith’s Pygmalion explored representing and developing procedures visually, including demonstrating operations on examples. The aim was to bring programming closer to the way someone works out a problem. It is one historical reason to avoid saying that plain-language AI was the first attempt to remove the need to type a conventional program. Later systems tried demonstration, block assembly and direct editing as different ways in. N05 J30 J51

In 1979 Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston brought VisiCalc to the Apple II. Start with a paper budget: when the quantity of an item changes, you erase its cost, then erase the total, then redo both calculations. In a spreadsheet you put quantities and prices in cells and make the total depend on those cells. Change one price and the sheet recalculates. The spreadsheet authors had to build cells, references, formulas and recalculation. They did not have to foresee your department’s travel budget. This was a commercial application, not a hypothetical machine. R08

Now test your objection: “But the developer still chose the formulas.” Yes. A formula language sets limits. Within those limits you can express a relationship no menu designer specifically provided. Entering five quantities is content entry. Writing a rule that flags a budget whenever the total exceeds the grant is creating reusable behavior. Adding an entirely new kind of editor is a third, deeper change. Asking which of these powers a user needs tells us more than debating whether a spreadsheet is simply open or closed. R08 N12 R60

What Kay’s 1984 paper actually does with a spreadsheet. Imagine that your spreadsheet has no built-in button for making the bar chart you want. Kay shows how a grid can become a chart anyway. Treat each cell as a tiny square of display and give the cells a rule for when to appear dark. A column of dark squares becomes a bar. Calculate the scale from the largest value so that entering a new, larger number changes the scale of the entire picture. The designer supplied cells and rules, but did not have to supply this particular chart as a feature. This is stronger than “different people type different numbers.” The person has made the sheet behave like a tool for drawing. That is the link from Kay’s article to your banana counter. R09

1983 to 1988 A pointable object, a box, a card and a model

Ben Shneiderman’s 1983 article and the 1985 analysis by Hutchins, Hollan and Norman explored direct manipulation. Dragging a shape instead of typing coordinates puts the object, the action and the feedback close together. An important nuance: a slider is excellent for adjusting a quantity the designer exposed, but it cannot by itself say “create a relationship between attendance and food quantities.” Direct manipulation and a language for describing new rules solve different problems. Jelly will eventually use both. N07 N09 R40

In 1986 Andrea diSessa and Harold Abelson described Boxer, a computing medium built around visible, nestable boxes. Data and procedures can inhabit the same environment. Picture a box representing an experiment with its measurements and rules inside; opening it reveals things you can work on rather than a sealed movie of the result. Like Smalltalk, Boxer asks whether a learner can construct the medium being used for learning. The visible organizational unit is different: a box is a place in which to see or compose more structure. R10

Bill Atkinson’s HyperCard, released for Macintosh in 1987, offered a more concrete starting place: a stack of cards. Put a question on one card, an answer on another, add a button that navigates between them, then add a script to keep score. A novice could browse; a maker could draw, add fields and buttons, and eventually write HyperTalk. That is how a document becomes a small application: it responds to actions according to rules you supplied. The user did not rewrite the vendor’s HyperCard program. Apple also made Knowledge Navigator, a concept video of a future assistant. The card environment shipped; the imagined assistant in the video was a vision. R11 J06 J08 R43

In 1988 Glenn Krasner and Stephen Pope described model–view–controller in Smalltalk-80. A simple reading is enough: the model contains the information; a view shows it; interaction changes it. A list of tasks and a calendar can show the same deadline. Changing the deadline should update both views. This is one of the most useful direct links to Jelly: the Jelly authors actually cite this work. They ask what happens if an AI helps change even the kind of information in the model. J27 R40

1989 to 2011 Why linking information was easier than sharing behavior

The Web solved one part of the problem at CERN

At CERN, people came and went, projects changed, and information about a piece of work could be known by someone in another group. Berners-Lee’s 1989 memorandum proposed linking information already living on different machines. By the end of 1990, a working browser/editor and server demonstrated the idea. A server answers requests for resources; a browser can request a resource and follow a link to another server. The next document could be on another machine under a different person’s care. N10 N11

This supplies the most important correction to the “one app” story: the Web succeeded at connecting without requiring central ownership of every item. It did not make every page editable by every reader. Linking to the university’s grade form is easy; changing another person’s mark requires authority, a shared understanding of what a mark means, and a record of who changed it. A link solves none of those three problems. This distinction between finding, combining, and acting explains why a Web of tools is a harder proposition than a Web of pages.

Changing a tool became a social as well as a technical question

In 1990 Allan MacLean and colleagues studied Buttons, a user-tailorable environment. Consider the distance between receiving a useful button from a colleague, changing what it opens and writing its behavior from scratch. All three are customization. If the first takes a click and the next requires becoming a full-time programmer, most people stop at the first. The researchers’ idea of a gentle slope was to make intermediate steps available. It did not mean that expertise would disappear. R12

Nardi and Miller’s 1991 study of spreadsheet work is valuable because it changes the protagonist. The inventor of a sheet, the colleague who understands a difficult formula and the person who uses the sheet every day can be different people. They can still develop the tool together. Bonnie Nardi’s 1993 book places that activity within end-user computing. Imagine that you can edit your timer’s duration and that one lab partner knows how to add a pause button. The question for the designer is whether what your partner makes can be inspected, adapted and passed on. The alternative to a vendor doing everything is not necessarily every individual learning everything. N12 J40

By 1994 Pattie Maes was studying software agents that assisted users with information work. An agent was not invented by ChatGPT. What changed later was the breadth of ordinary-language requests that a model could interpret, and the ease of connecting a model to tools. This historical correction matters to your research: you can investigate how delegated authority changes with today’s systems without claiming older software never acted on anyone’s behalf. N13 R36

Three ways of getting beyond one big application

1. Embed the work of a second tool. Apple’s 1990s OpenDoc framework organized documents into parts with appropriate editors. Imagine changing a numerical table in the body of a report rather than switching to a separate spreadsheet document, exporting an image and pasting it back. Microsoft’s OLE compound documents offer a related commercial example. The cooperation works because programs agree on a way to provide and host a part. Merely wishing that a spreadsheet and a report should cooperate does not create that agreement. J07 R61

2. Organize information around the owner instead of around file types. MIT’s Haystack (1997 white paper; 1999 prototype paper by Adar, Karger and Stein) explored a personal repository and relationships among objects. Think of a person who remembers “the budget Alice sent for the trip” rather than the filename. A system representing the relationship among Alice, the trip and the budget has a better starting point than a list of filenames. This puts your “one place for my work” idea on firm historical ground. The evidence is a research prototype, not an industry-wide service or proof that sharing everything is harmless. J23 J03

3. Separate a tool from the objects it can act upon. Michel Beaudouin-Lafon’s 2000 work on instrumental interaction treats an instrument of interaction and the thing it acts on as distinct. A physical pen can mark several kinds of paper. Could a digital commenting tool attach to a drawing as well as a text paragraph? To do that, the comment needs an address for the particular thing it refers to. See what happens if “comment on paragraph 3” is stored literally and someone inserts a new opening paragraph. Reusable tools require stable ways to identify their targets. Patchwork’s later experiments make this question tangible. N14 R38 R43

A second research family tried to generate the controls themselves

In parallel with user authoring, interface researchers asked how much of a screen a computer could construct from a description. Robert Jacob’s 1983 work on formal specifications, MIKE (1986), ITS (1990), UIDE (1991), HUMANOID (1992–93), and later model-based interface frameworks all appear in Jelly’s bibliography. Their common principle is simple: tell a system what information or operations exist and let rules help produce the controls. The work differs in what the human had to specify, when decisions were made and what the generator chose. In much of this strand the person supplying the model was a developer. Giving a developer a faster way to build a screen is not the same as giving the eventual customer control over it. J21 J48 J67 J13 J58 J34 J50

Two appliance/interface projects make the design choice easier to see. Jeffrey Nichols and colleagues investigated generating remotes from descriptions of what appliances could do. Huddle (2006) went further: descriptions of connected devices helped generate controls for a system of devices. A television and receiver may each offer a volume control; the useful interface for watching a film depends on which one actually handles the sound. In SUPPLE, Krzysztof Gajos and colleagues studied automatically choosing interfaces to suit devices and people’s abilities. A small target that suits one person may be awkward for another to point at. Here, changing the layout can change who can use the software at all. Neither project needed a large language model. J43 J44 J45 J46 J16 J18 J17 J68

Two comparisons are easy to defend. Huddle is close to the idea of making several independent things feel like one task, but only within the devices and descriptions it understands. SUPPLE gives users the benefit of an adapted interface, but benefiting from an automatic choice is different from owning the rules that select it. When Jelly arrives, ask whether its user can change the underlying description as well as the screen.

If the owner does not provide extensions, what can the user still do?

C3W (2004) investigated clipping and connecting material from the Web. Vegemite (2009) combined tables with demonstrations so that a person could assemble information from several sites and automate web operations. Prefab (2010) explored recognizing interface structures from their rendered pixels and attaching new behaviors. Later, Fusion (2018) let people combine elements from existing Web interfaces in a prototype. These are different routes to adaptation: use a documented connection, work with the structure a page exposes, or infer structure from its appearance. They differ in fragility as well as power. J15 J30 J12 J75

Imagine a bus timetable. One tool reads a published “departure time” field. Another looks for text in the third column. A third recognizes the shape of the timetable on screen. All might display today’s next bus correctly. Tomorrow the website adds an advertisement before column three. Which tool is likely to mistake the advertisement for a departure? That question is more revealing than asking which demonstration looked better. It is also why a universal agent that simply “looks at any screen and edits the app” is not the same as a supported extension system.

Meta-design (Fischer and colleagues, 2004) names the decision to design for later design by others. Situated software (Shirky, 2004) asks what changes when software is made for a particular group rather than a mass market. Ko and colleagues studied learning barriers in end-user programming and later surveyed end-user software engineering. Once people construct and rely on their own rules, explaining, testing and repairing those rules become part of the work. A group-shared banana counter that silently misses “two bananas” illustrates the point: enabling creation creates a need to establish what the tool actually does. R14 N15 J26 R16

2011 to 2021 Put the material and the tools within reach

A view can explain a rule that words alone obscure

Bret Victor’s 2011 interactive Ladder of Abstraction lets a reader move between individual cases and views over many cases. Imagine looking at a single run of a timer versus a graph of every start and pause. The second view may reveal a defect hidden by the first. The important move is letting a person change the representation while retaining a connection to the same behavior. This is a precursor by comparison, not a claim that every later visualization descended from one essay. N17

In 2015 Clemens Klokmose and colleagues built Webstrates. A Web page has an underlying tree of elements: a heading contains text, a list contains items, and so on. A webstrate synchronizes changes to the document structure between clients. The page can act as shared editable material, not merely as a display downloaded from a server. In 2017 Codestrates, by Roman Rädle and colleagues, built a literate computing environment on top of Webstrates: prose, editable code and its results could live in a shared computational document. These two are a documented platform-and-environment relationship. A 2023 retrospective from the research community is a useful check on the distance between a promising principle and living with the tools. R17 R18 R31

Try a group-notebook thought experiment. Alice edits the text of a note and Bob sees it. That is shared content. Alice edits code that generates a chart and Bob sees the new chart. That is shared behavior. Alice installs a private reading aid and Bob’s display remains unchanged. That is different shared behavior: the system has a way to distinguish their scopes. The first two properties do not automatically provide the third. “Everyone sees all edits” can be a bug for your project.

Dynamicland explored a more radical setting: people in a physical room work with computational objects on surfaces rather than retreating to separate personal screens. The laboratory’s 2018 presentation documents the idea. A useful contrast with Webstrates is what counts as a shared workspace: synchronized browser documents in one case, people and physical objects present together in the other. It is a working research environment, not an app you install to transform a home into a lab. R19 J66

2019 A particularly important predecessor to your project

Before treating “malleable software” as an invention of the recent AI wave, read Philip Tchernavskij’s 2019 dissertation. It is explicitly about designing and programming malleable software. He developed Tangler to explore interactions assembled as components become available. In his terminology an entanglement connects parts of an interaction; an entangler establishes such connections when the appropriate conditions occur. The dissertation describes constructed benchmark cases for changes made by people alone or with programmer help. Ink & Switch cites it more than once. N18 R43

Here is an analogy you can draw on a board. In a fixed notepad, the developer wires a particular counter button to one particular note. In a more composable design, a rule says: “When an item that supplies a quantity and a display that accepts a quantity are both present, connect them.” You can now replace the display without writing the whole note again. That is our translation of the design issue, not a claim that Tangler contained a banana counter. The difficult parts are deciding which pieces count as compatible, what happens when one disappears, and who may make a new connection. That last question is where your authority research can contribute a different test.

In the same year Szymon Kaliski, Adam Wiggins and James Lindenbaum described Ink & Switch’s Capstone experiments in their essay on end-user programming. They tried exposing a card’s source, connecting data in pipelines and providing hooks or bots for automation. Imagine editing a rule beside the card it affects and seeing the result immediately. This already separated two problems: making editing convenient and giving editors a stable vocabulary of operations they can understand. Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg and McGranaghan’s local-first paper addressed a different obstacle: what is the value of a personal tool if your working copy disappears with a server or the network? Local-first means aiming for a useful local copy with collaboration and synchronization; it does not prohibit cloud services, and it does not by itself supply encryption, portability of every format or authorization for every feature. N19 R20

2019 and 2020 Three bottlenecks hidden behind the word integration

Finding a usable connection. Litt and Jackson’s Wildcard exposed selected website data as a table people could manipulate; related work with Millis and Quaye studied direct manipulation of tabular data. A programmer writes an adapter that identifies meaningful things on a particular site and connects them to table rows and columns. Think of a course page that displays a title, a deadline and a status for each assignment. Once those fields are exposed, a student can build a priority column without understanding the website’s entire code. A different website may need a different adapter. This is how a general editing idea can coexist with very specific integration work. R22 R23

Keeping changes when people work apart. Ink & Switch’s PushPin explored a shared canvas of objects with peer-to-peer collaboration. A note and an image can be placed on the same board, and collaborators need changes to reach one another later. Automerge supplies data structures that reconcile concurrent edits to supported structures. That is useful machinery, but convergence means the machines agree on a result, not that two people’s intentions never conflict. Two people can both rename a research category for good but incompatible reasons. Farm is a related experimental environment in the lab’s history; its repository and the lab’s account are the right evidence for its status. R24 R58 R59 R43

Agreeing about meaning. Ink & Switch’s Cambria explored translating data between different schema versions using lenses. A schema is an agreement about what fields mean. Suppose your notebook used the field “shop,” while a new tool expects “store.” The string “Corner Market” remains in the file, but the new tool sees no value at the location it knows how to read. A translation rule can present “shop” as “store.” Splitting a full name into first and last is a more difficult case because the split is ambiguous. Choosing a shared file format solves surprisingly little unless changes in meaning have an owner. Cambria was a research prototype, not a promise to repair every incompatible update. R21

In 2020 Robin Sloan described an app made for a tiny, known group. The point of his home-cooked app was that an audience of a few can still justify making software, as cooking dinner for four justifies cooking. In a vendor relationship, the economic question is who keeps the kitchen running: if the custom behavior breaks next semester, who diagnoses and repairs it? Small-scale value and long-term maintenance are both real. N20 R16

2021 to 2024 Let a document acquire behavior while someone is using it

Sketching and writing start from something people already know how to do

Ink & Switch’s Inkbase explored programmable hand-drawn marks; related work appeared at LIVE 2021 and in the lab’s longer account. Untangle explored expressing everyday constraints with marks on a tablet and inspecting possible solutions. Think about arranging people at a table: the drawing is easy until someone says two guests must sit together. Giving that relationship a representation changes what the sketch can do for you. The connection to Sketchpad is visible, and the Inkbase authors themselves discuss Sutherland. In another strand, Varv (2022) represented interactive software as declarative data: pieces describe concepts and behavior a runtime can combine or extend. Varv attacks the programming foundation; programmable ink attacks the experience of working in a familiar medium. N21 N22 R27 R03

2022 Potluck starts with a note you already have

Geoffrey Litt, Max Schoening, Paul Shen and Paul Sonnentag’s Potluck asked a small but consequential question: why must a person abandon a perfectly good note and migrate into a special app the moment they need one calculation? Their prototype searches freeform text for patterns, calculates with the extracted information and puts results or interactive annotations back next to the writing. The report explores recipes, calculations and timers, among other examples. Its core is a working text-and-computation prototype; exploratory AI examples should not be confused with a general autonomous editor. R25

Write these three lines in an imaginary note: “bananas: 3”, “milk: 1”, “bananas: 4”. A pattern finds the two banana lines. A calculation adds the numbers to get 7; counting occurrences of the word would incorrectly produce 2 for this purpose. An annotation displays “7 bananas” beside the note. If you change 4 to 5 and it now displays 8, you have demonstrated behavior, not a picture of behavior. If a user enters “half a dozen bananas,” our simple pattern may miss it. That is a fact about the rule we chose, not a failure of arithmetic.

The authors link a Potluck demo and a gallery of examples. Open the recipe example and look for the point at which editing ordinary text changes a calculated result.

Why isn’t this just writing JavaScript in VS Code? Both can involve real programming. Where they differ is what the environment already supplies. In a blank code editor you must arrange for a note to exist, for changes to be detected, and for results to appear on the screen. In Potluck, your calculation participates in an existing document loop. Your criticism still stands: a difficult pattern or calculation can require expertise. The research claim is about lowering the cost of an incremental change, not about making every possible change equally easy. R25 R12

2023 Embark starts with things that the note refers to

Paul Sonnentag, Alexander Obenauer and Geoffrey Litt’s Embark explored planning with an outline. One line can be ordinary prose. Typing an @ mention and choosing a real place inserts a reference to a structured object; a place can have coordinates. A map view reads places in the surrounding outline. Formulas can use these same objects in other computations. The authors tried the prototype on real trips. They also describe limits, including implicit agreements about the shape of data. R35

Take the same Saturday in Houston and try it both ways. Potluck: write “museum, 10:00; café, 12:00,” teach a rule to find the times, and show your gap between appointments. Embark: write the same outline, deliberately select the two named venues as place mentions, and insert a map view that shows both pins using their coordinates. Type a vague name without selecting a location and you have not necessarily given the map a place it can plot. Weather for a plan also requires a date, a location and a source of weather data. A view inside a note need not mean the note application owns or independently provides a weather service. You still decide where to go. In the original report, an assistant that could plan an itinerary is discussed as an exploratory direction, not the defining mechanism. R25 R35

This example gets very close to your opening story. You do not want all of Google Maps, all of a calendar and all of a weather app fused together. You want two places and a date to remain meaningful when several tools look at the same trip. A contact list, grades and banking records have no part in that task.

Language models lowered one cost and exposed several others

Litt’s 2023 essay on malleability in the age of LLMs made an argument about the cost of personal software: a small tool can become worth making if turning an intention into code gets cheaper. He later described a personal translation-tool experiment. That is evidence that a person made a particular tool, not evidence that every non-programmer can maintain one. Studies of code generation by Vaithilingam and colleagues and by Barke and colleagues help explain why: deciding whether a suggestion does the intended thing and debugging it remain real tasks. Earlier work such as PUMICE already combined language and demonstration in a bounded setting. R33 N24 R26 R30 J29

AI Chains exposed intermediate steps in an LLM workflow. Spellburst gave creative coders a node-based environment for exploring generated program alternatives. Think of asking for a gentler animation, keeping both versions and deciding by looking at their results. DynaVis (2024) took a different route: ask for an edit to a visualization and get a persistent control for repeating or adjusting it. The first request might be “make these labels larger”; thereafter a slider can be better than five more chat messages. UICoder studied training models to improve generated interface code through automatic feedback. Code that renders, a control you can adjust repeatedly, and alternatives you can compare are three different achievements. R28 R29 J63 J69

ReAct and Toolformer studied using tools with language models. Calling an existing function, writing a new function and installing one for another user are different operations. For example, “start my existing timer” uses a capability, “make a timer that pauses in meetings” defines a new behavior, and “install it for the whole department” changes other people’s environment. The last request might be only a few more words but it crosses an entirely different boundary. R36 R34

Patchwork and the question of who sees an experiment

Farm and Patchwork belong to Ink & Switch’s longer investigation of personal and collaborative tools. Patchwork explores version control for materials beyond conventional source code. Take a shared essay. In the main version the introduction is intact. You create a branch, rewrite the opening, and compare the alternatives. A collaborator can consider bringing the change back. A branch is a distinct version; it is not inherently private, and it is not inherently a separate complete application installed on every laptop. Who can see a branch depends on how the particular system handles access. R38 R59 N35

Why does this matter for a generated extension? Suppose two lab members ask for opposite defaults: hide completed tasks, and always show completed tasks. A chat transcript records that two requests were made. It does not decide whose preference takes effect. Private views, group defaults, histories and explicit merges are ways to express the difference. The appealing iPhone analogy is that a common update can coexist with personal settings. The research question begins precisely where that analogy stops: what if the update removes an operation that your custom timer used? Saving the old preference and making it work in the new host are two separate duties.

2025 Two routes converge on the user’s task

What Ink and Switch means by malleable software

In June 2025 Geoffrey Litt, Josh Horowitz, Peter van Hardenberg and Todd Matthews organized years of work into the essay Malleable Software. Its central problem is familiar to anyone who has joined a workplace with a standard tool: choosing software also means adopting some of somebody else’s working habits. Think of replacing a team’s wall of movable index cards with an issue tracker that offers only “open” and “closed.” The tracker can be faster to search while making the team’s important third state harder to express. Their essay describes an agenda for tools that people can adapt with less friction. It is a synthesis of examples and prototypes, not a controlled trial across all software. R43

The essay offers three ways to recognize progress. A gentle slope: start with a useful thing, adjust it, then learn a little more only if needed. Tools that compose: an operation should work with meaningful material from elsewhere when it makes sense to do so. Communal creation: someone in a group can make a change others benefit from without appealing to a distant vendor. Read Buttons for the first, Webstrates or Embark for the second, and Nardi and Miller or Sloan for the third. These links are more useful than memorizing a string of product names. R12 R17 R35 N12 N20

One revealing detail is what this agenda does not settle. Who pays when an extension serving three people breaks after an update? Can a personal view be shared without sharing the underlying private records? Can another developer understand and repair an AI-generated rule? Those are reasons for research; they are not predictions that all vendors will adopt one system. See the Ink & Switch source trail for the essay’s other examples, including its references to modding, macro systems, reusable instruments, programmable ink and small-group software.

Jelly changes the description from which the screen is drawn

Yining Cao, Peiling Jiang and Haijun Xia built Jelly for their CHI 2025 paper. Start with a dinner party, their example. A chat can return a plan. A code generator can create a page that displays one. Jelly first builds a task data model: what kinds of things are involved, what information each holds and how changes relate. Its system maps that model to an interactive interface. The user can request another change or directly manipulate the result. In the implementation, a Python pipeline and React front end work with model-generated structured descriptions; some dependency mechanisms can include JavaScript. Calling it a system that “never generates any code” would be inaccurate. R40

Look at the figure before you read the next paragraph. The panels belong to a single research prototype. They are not unrelated applications it has opened. Imagine that each panel is a different question you can ask of the same dinner plan: Who is coming? What will they eat? What do we still need? When one item appears in several panels, the underlying references matter more than the windows. Open the paper’s Figure 4 to see the labeled controls. R40 R64

Try a fresh example on paper. Draw a rectangle called Paper. Inside it put title and year. Add two actual paper titles. You have just distinguished the schema (“what a paper can contain”) from the data (“which two papers I have”). Draw a second rectangle called Meeting. Give it a date and a link to one or more papers. Now say: “Show me which meeting has readings I haven’t checked.” To implement that request you need a checked field, a relationship connecting each meeting with its readings, and a view that shows a warning. A rectangle on screen cannot tell you whether the program has those three pieces.

Now change the task. “Actually, I want to track whether I checked each claim, not just each paper.” Adding a checkbox to a paper is insufficient: one paper can contain several claims. You have to add a new kind of thing, Claim, and connect each claim to a paper. That is what it means to reshape a data model. An application that lets you add as many paper titles as you want but never add a new kind of thing offers a different level of agency. This is an original teaching example; it is not a result from Jelly’s study.

What evidence did the team actually collect?

Question What the researchers examined What you can reasonably say
Did the model propose sensible structure? 25 generated information tasks, two prompt detail levels each; 50 models containing 197 entities, 1,052 attributes and 232 dependencies. Coders labeled roughly 94–95% of generated entities and attributes “necessary and expected.” This describes judgments about generated elements, not a test of every possible missing field.
Did it connect the right things in the right way? The team coded the direction/relationship and its validation or update mechanism separately. The reported average accuracies were 91.5% for relationships and 96.9% for mechanisms. A system can connect the wrong fields even when its calculation runs.
Could people revise an interface? Eight daily users of generative AI; guided introduction and short open-ended tasks. Logs covered 14 of 16 tasks; 120 follow-up messages became 131 coded prompts. Authors reported three failures among those 120 messages. That denominator is not the number of people, tasks or generated programs. It is not a general product reliability rate.

Read sections 7–9 of the paper alongside the table. It does not show that a university can install Jelly over all its apps, enforce the role of every employee, or preserve all edits across future vendor releases. Inspecting external/personal data and handling more complex dependencies are among the issues the researchers discuss. The authors link a model-evaluation viewer for examining the evaluated models. A results viewer and a video are different from an installable public release of the full prototype. R40 R64

Jelly has more than one historical family

Earlier approach Who supplied the structure? What Jelly helps us ask
HyperCard, Smalltalk, Boxer A human authors behavior within a prepared medium. Can a person who cannot script still make a structural change?
MVC, ITS, HUMANOID, SUPPLE Designers specify information, actions or constraints; a system can generate or select views. What happens if the user’s task can change the model as well as the view?
C3W, Vegemite, Fusion, Wildcard Existing web content is exposed, demonstrated or adapted into a workable form. Where does the model get real information, and who maintains the connection?
Haystack, Potluck, Embark Material from a person’s work is organized as objects or enriched in place. Can ordinary language revise the information structure during the task?
DynaVis and generated UI code A specification or program yields visible controls. Will the third request preserve the meaning established by the first two?

Smalltalk, HyperCard, Wildcard, Embark, DynaVis and the model-based work are explicit references in Jelly; Potluck and Boxer are conceptual comparisons in this row grouping. The distinction matters: similarity is evidence for grouping literature, not proof of intellectual influence. R40 R25 R10

Other 2025 research changed different parts of the problem

Malleable Overview-Detail Interfaces and Meridian are related but different papers. Imagine buying a couch: the product list emphasizes pictures and prices; you need width and fabric because the couch must pass through a narrow door. You want to pull a property from each details page into the overview and compare items there. The CHI paper investigates changes of this kind. The UIST paper by Bryan Min and Haijun Xia introduces Meridian, a design framework and shared specification that connects authoring tools and the running interface. Jelly starts from a task and generates a model; Meridian starts from a recognizable family of interfaces and asks how designers, developers and end users can reshape them. R45 R44

Denicek by Tomas Petricek and Jonathan Edwards represents a document program as the edits that construct and transform it. Its machinery can apply edits, merge histories and resolve conflicts; the authors exercised it by building a data science notebook. Ambsheets by Alex Warth, Geoffrey Litt and Avi Bryant explores a different problem: a spreadsheet cell can hold alternatives, so a user can inspect a family of scenarios. Enter two possible rents and two commuting costs and see what each pairing does to a monthly budget. Denicek preserves a history of changes; Ambsheets keeps alternatives present for a calculation. Neither requires an LLM to illustrate a gain in agency. R47 R48

2026 What happens after the first good demonstration

The most interesting question by 2026 is no longer just “can a model draw a screen?” Consider a student’s response to the first version of a study dashboard: “I didn’t know I wanted to group papers by question until I saw them grouped by author; now please keep my grouping next week.” Discovering a preference, expressing it, remembering it, applying it to the next version and testing the result are five separate research problems. The works below give different pieces of the answer. Dates for arXiv records refer to the public manuscript; they are not automatically publication dates in a journal.

Public milestone What the work contributes What that looks like for a reader
January: Gradual Generation Min, Jiang, Huang and Xia present intermediate stages of UI generation, with controls at different stages and a way to wind back. They demonstrate the approach through three prototype sites. R53 Revisit the choice of grouping without having to know the right prompt in advance.
April: Generative UI / PAGEN Leviathan and colleagues evaluate generated interactive answers, including human preference and expert-created examples. The comparison with static text sets aside generation speed in a key result. N31 Someone may prefer an interactive explanation today. That alone says nothing about whether they can keep and repair it tomorrow.
April: From Words to Widgets Zhang and colleagues turn expressed preferences into reusable controls and modulate generation according to their values. N30 Ask once for more emphasis on evidence; use a control to vary that preference instead of rewriting the entire request.
April: ALADDIN Wang and colleagues investigate generating functional tests from a user’s requirement, using six mobile apps for their benchmark. R57 A visible timer button is not enough. Does pausing stop the count? That is a behavioral test.
May: Conversational Customization Sreedhar, Kaul and Chilton use a customizable email system as a design probe in people’s workflows over several days. Users often adapted familiar patterns. R56 A person may ask for “my existing inbox rule, except for seminar notices,” rather than inventing a new app.
2026 doctoral symposium: documentation review Bhat draws on interviews with 31 technical writers and proposes malleable views for different reviewers. The evaluations of the proposed system are future work in this paper. N32 A reviewer can need a terminology view while an engineer needs a technical-changes view. A proposal for such a tool is not a completed trial.
August: Maru Kim and colleagues persist rules about grouping, hierarchy, order and vocabulary across generations. R52 “Draft” means something specific in your lab. The next model-generated view should keep that meaning and organization.
September: Elicitive User Interfaces Kim and colleagues explore generating the way the interface asks for preferences, supported by two studies with a design probe. R51 Show two ways to organize a reading list and let the person choose rather than demanding a perfect written specification.
October: MalleableSpace Chen and colleagues report a comparison of 58 papers and a three-month study of seven experienced agent users. Their prototype and model focus on shared representations of work. R49 A research question, its evidence and an unresolved disagreement can remain visible to both researcher and agent after the chat has scrolled away.
November 2: The Personalized Computer for the 21st Century A UIST 2026 workshop program documents an active research conversation. A workshop is evidence of the questions a community is asking, not a single validated solution. N33 The personal computer is again being discussed in terms of whose preferences and purposes actually shape it.

Compare three meanings of “keep my change.” In Maru, a preference about organization survives another generation. In Patchwork, a version can remain available for comparison. In Cambria, a representation can be translated so a different tool can still interpret data. All three involve persistence. They protect different things. A vendor promising to preserve customizations should specify which promise it is making. R52 R38 R21

What differential agency adds

Two questions that sound similar until a person needs to act

Malleability asks what the working tool can become and what it costs the user to change it. Differential agency, as used in your research project, asks how authority over that change is divided. Fix the product, the deployment, the person and the task. “This software is open” leaves most of that sentence unfinished. A university can have the right to obtain code but no right to change a vendor’s live service. A student can add a personal timer without being able to alter the course deadline. A vendor can maintain the host while a department owns its notes. These are not contradictions.

The private class framework distinguishes source access, execution control, data sovereignty, extensibility, observability and delegated action scope. It also separates what someone controls from the role the software itself plays. A tool can be easily changed by its owner and do very little on its own. A highly proactive hosted assistant can suggest or execute a great deal while the customer has little power over its internals. Treat the proposed 0–10 profiles as design claims requiring evidence; a 7 for one capability does not imply a 7 for another. The public research survey needs neither the private manuscript nor its figures to make and test this distinction.

Ask about one university notepad deployment Evidence you could actually show
Source: can this customer inspect and build the relevant part? Build the extension from the available source. Record separately whether the host’s source is available.
Execution: where can this customer run it? Disconnect the network, reopen a saved note and run the local counter. Check the optional AI feature separately.
Data: what can the customer take away or remove? Export notes and rules; open them in a fresh instance. Check whether deletion includes synced or retained copies before promising it.
Extension: which new behaviors can they create or replace? Add a new rule after release. Show whether only preinstalled choices are possible, or genuinely new rules within the supported language.
Observation: can the responsible person reconstruct a change? Display what changed, its scope, who approved it and the previous version, without exposing the private note just to create a log.
Delegation: what can software do on whose behalf? An assistant proposes a feature. Can it also install, share or send data? Demonstrate separate outcomes for each operation.

That table is an assessment instrument, not an Angular-like package or a command window. An implementation might display it using evidence collected from a host, its declared extension permissions and reproducible tests. A list of eight actions in a workflow is not on its own proof of differential agency. Evidence arises when you vary the actor or the permitted operation and document what really changes. Unknown is an honest result; it should not silently become zero or ten.

The public literature on authority is a parallel track

Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 security work includes least privilege: a tool should have the rights needed for its task. Sandhu and colleagues’ role-based access control relates permissions to roles. Miller’s 2006 work on capabilities studies how components can collaborate with limited authority; hardware research such as CHERI addresses a different enforcement layer. Roles answer, for instance, why a teacher can submit grades. A capability might let one counter read one derived quantity, without giving it a general route to the rest of a notebook. None of those mechanisms tells you whether a teacher without programming experience can create a new kind of annotation or whether it survives next semester’s update. R06 R13 N16 N36

Open source generally concerns the license for code, including rights to use, modify and redistribute it under its terms. It does not mean an ordinary user of a hosted installation may change other users’ records. The GNU AGPL’s network-use provision concerns offering corresponding source under its conditions; it is not a general right to export one’s data, audit production logs, or inspect everyone else’s transactions. Widder and colleagues examine material limits on openness claims in AI. White and colleagues’ Model Openness Framework distinguishes multiple components of an AI release. These are genuine neighbors: both resist a misleading single label. Their object of analysis is not identical to a particular customer’s authority over a deployed application. R39 R15 N23 N25 N26

Differential privacy is a different kind of concept. The formal guarantee concerns how much the distribution of outputs changes when one person’s data changes. In a university survey, a mechanism might add calibrated noise to a count before releasing it. A role check controls who gets to run the report; the privacy guarantee concerns what releasing the result reveals. Using graded language about agency is not enough to borrow the mathematical guarantee of differential privacy. N38 R68

Finally, making a model more capable does not answer how far it should act. Chan and colleagues study agent visibility, Feng and colleagues propose levels of autonomy, and security work including AgentDojo and CaMeL examines risks and defenses around tool-using models. The user-facing distinction is easy to state: “show me a proposed change,” “apply it to my copy,” and “publish it to the team” are three different authorizations. A log records an event; it does not authorize it. An explanation written by a model is not the same as a record produced by the system that actually performed the action. N27 N29 R37 N28 R46 R32

Serval is a useful comparison precisely because it is different

In the Serval discussion, the starting point was an employee trying to get work done. The official documentation describes triage, access requests, approval flows and automation. Think of a request to join an approved project repository: a configured workflow could route it to the appropriate approver and invoke the relevant integration. That is more than filing a ticket. It is still different from the employee creating a new type of workflow, a new integration, or a personal tool the administrator did not previously offer. You would need evidence about that particular deployment to assert any of those things, especially persistence across a vendor update. Product documentation and the interview are product evidence, not an independent experiment. R63 R55

Imagine the same sentence in two products: “Remind me if this access request is still waiting after two days.” Product A already has a reminder feature and switches it on. Product B lets the team author a reusable trigger on pending requests, define who may receive it, inspect the logic and export it. Both may produce the same reminder. The agency differs when the team wants to change “two days” to “two working days,” move the rule to another installation, or revoke permission to send notifications. This is the kind of comparison that makes the term useful to a buyer or a designer.

A small experiment that follows from the history

Choose one vendor, one customer, one notepad. The vendor supplies a place to type and a place in which approved extensions appear. The customer is one university lab. Start without AI so you can measure what the host itself makes possible. Later add a language model as an alternative way to request the same supported operations. Your contribution is not inventing a timer or claiming that the notepad proves a theory about every application. It is making one agency difference visible, testable and explainable.

Step What to actually do What the observer learns
1. Establish a baseline Write “bananas: 3” and “bananas: 4.” Save and reopen. The user can edit content. The host has no counting behavior yet.
2. Add a rule Add a sidebar rule: extract quantities beside “bananas” and sum them. Change 4 to 5. The result should change from 7 to 8. A reusable behavior was added after the note existed.
3. Add a different kind of feature Add a five-minute timer with start and pause. Save its state separately from note text. A timer needs a clock and state. A timer on its own does not need the note, the network, or the entire repository.
4. Separate authority Permit the student to install personally. Require an authorized lab owner to publish a group default. Offer a preview, then undo. Identical software, different actors and scopes. Test with a second user who should see no personal change.
5. Ship a host update Keep the extension record; change a supported field in a test version. Supply an adapter or stop with a readable compatibility message. File persistence and functional compatibility are separately measurable. A skipped or incorrect total is a failure, even if the file remains.
6. Add natural-language authoring Ask the agent for the same counter; have it propose a bounded rule the host checks and previews. Compare with a hand-authored rule. A better input method and more delegated authority can be varied independently. The model does not get to grant itself extra permission.

What an update could look like. The host stores the note, a separate extension definition, an extension version, its selected scope, and timer state. A compatible update to the common host can keep using those records without building a whole new vendor program for every user. If the host changes what an extension is allowed to read, recheck the old permission; do not silently widen it to make an update appear successful. If the requested operation no longer exists, retain the note and old configuration, explain the mismatch and offer a reversible migration. Local storage is one possible implementation; it is not what guarantees agency. The guarantee depends on the actual storage, enforcement, recovery and tests.

A defensible experiment. Compare the same host with a menu of fixed add-ons, a small editable rule language, and a natural-language assistant that proposes rules in that language. Give all versions the same permission boundary. Ask users to count bananas, then count only unpurchased bananas, then share the rule without sharing the list. Record task completion, wrong totals, whether users can explain the rule, accidental changes to someone else’s view, and successful recovery after an update. Record failures and cases not supported. This comparison can tell you something that a “no security versus security” comparison cannot: whether a form of authoring increases useful control when the security boundary is held constant. These are proposed tests, not study results.

A spoken close for the professor

“Bush asked how I could keep my own path through knowledge. Engelbart and Sutherland showed that a computer could respond to changes in meaningful structure. Smalltalk, spreadsheets and HyperCard let the person using a tool describe some of its behavior. The Web made links travel between systems, but it didn’t make their behaviors interchangeable. Later researchers built shared documents, adapters and personal data models. Ink & Switch asks how those ideas can make everyday tools easier for people to change. Jelly shows a concrete new possibility: I can ask for a change to the structure behind a screen, and keep working with the result. My question is what happens after that request succeeds: whose copy changes, who can inspect or undo it, and will it still work after an update? I can test that in one small notepad.”

If the professor asks “What is novel?”, the strongest answer is narrower than claiming a new field: “Personalization, tailoring, role permissions and agent autonomy already have substantial literatures. I want to find out whether a profile tied to observable tasks can distinguish systems that appear equally customizable in a demo but give customers different control after deployment.” If existing methods answer that question well, reproducing that finding is useful. A novel name by itself is not a result.

A reading route for one hour

Minutes Open and look at this Answer before moving on
0–8 Bush’s essay and the NLS demonstration archive. R01 R04 Which one was imagined, which one ran, and what relationship did the person create?
8–16 Kay and Goldberg, then Buttons. R07 R12 What was the difference between using an environment and modifying a behavior inside it?
16–24 Tchernavskij’s thesis summary and the original 2025 Ink & Switch essay. N18 R43 Why can a system be open source yet costly for its own users to change?
24–33 The Potluck recipe and Embark trip walkthroughs. R25 R35 For the exact same sentence, what does a pattern extract and what does a place mention refer to?
33–45 Jelly: Figures 1 and 4, then sections 7 and 8. R40 Draw one entity, an attribute, a dependency and a view. Explain what the eight-person study did and did not measure.
45–52 A Cambria example and Maru’s opening figure. R21 R52 If someone says “my changes survived,” what survived: the data, the preference or the working feature?
52–60 The notepad experiment above, spoken without notes. Describe one permitted change, one blocked change and one observable result after an update.

A useful reading habit: for each paper, write three lines on a card. **They actually built or studied . The evidence was . My project asks something different because ___.** If the second line is “they proposed it,” keep that answer. A research vision is evidence of what a person thought was worth pursuing; it is not proof that a solution already worked.

Source trails and selection

The starting points were the public Jelly paper (its March 2025 HTML reference list), the June 2025 Ink & Switch essay, and the 71-item public reading collection from the class discussions, including the shared videos. I checked the additional leads from the supplied outline against author, lab, publisher or archival records, with a targeted public search through 19 November 2026. The record year may be a release, a paper date or a retrospective: the distinction is noted where it affects the story. This is a backward citation trail and selected forward search, not an exhaustive systematic review of every publication in computing.

Provenance. R codes keep the numbering of the earlier reading collection; N codes identify additions. J codes index positions in Jelly’s bibliography and I codes index distinct textual reading/example links in the body of the Ink & Switch essay. These are four trails with overlaps, not four disjoint piles of independent research. A workshop schedule, product page, first-person essay and peer-reviewed study have different evidential roles. The bibliography file keeps scholarly references and visibly labeled discovery records; no private manuscript, figure or text is reproduced there.
