All 75 entries in Jelly’s bibliography

How to use this index. Core and Vision entries concern what can be shaped and by whom. Method entries explain a technical ingredient. Context, Product and Infrastructure entries tell you why a citation appears without turning it into evidence of user authority. These categories are this reader’s assessment. Each title leads to the source when a link is available or to the precise bibliography record where the citation can be traced. J37 and J38 duplicate the same Myers article in the authors’ list.

J01 · Context. Towards a better understanding of context and context-awareness (Abowd et al. (1999)). Defines context awareness: adapting to circumstances differs from letting a person author a change. Cited record.

J02 · Infrastructure. Gpt-4 technical report (Achiam et al. (2023)). Model report, cited for the AI machinery; not an end-user customization study. Cited record.

J03 · Core. Haystack: Per-user information environments (Adar et al. (1999)). Haystack puts personal information and its relationships at the center rather than organizing by app. Cited record.

J04 · Infrastructure. Claude-3.5 (Anthropic (2024)). The model supplier is implementation context, not evidence that the deployed interface is malleable. Cited record.

J05 · Infrastructure. Model Context Protocol (Anthropic (nd)). A common interface to external tools can enable data access; a connection does not grant permission. Cited record.

J06 · Vision. Knowledge Navigator (Apple Inc. (1987)). Concept film imagines an assistant; do not present it as a shipped 1987 agent. Cited record.

J07 · Core. OpenDoc (Apple Inc. (1995)). OpenDoc combines independently edited parts in a document; compare with Embark’s meaningful embeds. Cited record.

J08 · Core. Hypercard (Atkinson (1987)). HyperCard exposes fields, buttons and scripts so a document can become a small program. Cited record.

J09 · Method. Dashboard design patterns (Bach et al. (2022)). Dashboard design patterns help explain why a generator might select one familiar arrangement over another. Cited record.

J10 · Core. Compositional Structures as Substrates for Human-AI Co-creation Environment: A Design Approach and A Case Study (Cao et al. (2025)). A compositional structure can serve as common material for human and AI collaborators. Cited record.

J11 · Context. A conceptual framework and a toolkit for supporting the rapid prototyping of context-aware applications (Dey et al. (2001)). A toolkit supports context-sensitive applications; distinguish implicit adaptation from intentional editing. Cited record.

J12 · Core. Prefab: implementing advanced behaviors using pixel-based reverse engineering of interface structure (Dixon and Fogarty (2010)). Prefab infers structure from pixels to add interface behavior where the developer supplied no direct hook. Cited record.

J13 · Method. UIDE—an intelligent user interface design environment (Foley et al. (1991)). UIDE uses explicit design knowledge to construct interfaces. Ask who supplies the description. Cited record.

J14 · Core. Towards a dynamic multiscale personal information space: beyond application and document centered views of information (Fox et al. (2020)). Multiscale personal information spaces question why task material is split across separate tools. Cited record.

J15 · Core. C3W: clipping, connecting and cloning for the web (Fujima et al. (2004)). C3W lets a person clip and connect web material; a prior answer to the one-workspace question. Cited record.

J16 · Core. SUPPLE: automatically generating user interfaces (Gajos and Weld (2004)). SUPPLE studies automatically generating an interface from specifications and constraints. Cited record.

J17 · Core. Automatically generating personalized user interfaces with Supple (Gajos et al. (2010)). Extended treatment of personalized interface generation; a more powerful generator need not grant authorship. Cited record.

J18 · Core. Automatically generating user interfaces adapted to users’ motor and vision capabilities (Gajos et al. (2007)). Physical abilities can shape the generated interface; accessibility is a concrete reason one size fails. Cited record.

J19 · Method. Declarative language design for interactive visualization (Heer and Bostock (2010)). A declarative language can describe a graphic without making its author program every drawing operation. Cited record.

J20 · Method. Interactive specification of flexible user interface displays (Hudson and Mohamed (1990)). Flexible display specifications put design choices in a manipulable description rather than hard-coded pixels. Cited record.

J21 · Core. Using formal specifications in the design of a human-computer interface (Jacob (1983)). Formal interface descriptions predate LLMs; a computer can use a specified model, not just visual appearance. Cited record.

J22 · Context. Computational Approaches for Understanding, Generating, and Adapting User Interfaces (Jiang et al. (2022)). Review of computational understanding of interfaces; background on how machines recover screen structure. Cited record.

J23 · Core. Haystack: Per-User Information Environments (Karger and Stein (1997)). Earlier Haystack white paper; pair with the 1999 account rather than confusing it with a second product. Cited record.

J24 · Core. The early history of Smalltalk (Kay (1996)). Kay’s retrospective on Smalltalk. The year of a retrospective is not the year the system was invented. The linked author text also circulated in an earlier conference version. Cited record.

J25 · Context. Tangible user interface input: Tools and techniques (Klemmer (2004)). Tangible input is relevant to different physical media but peripheral to Jelly’s main data-model contribution. Cited record.

J26 · Core. Six learning barriers in end-user programming systems (Ko et al. (2004)). Six learning barriers show why exposing a language is not enough to make creation easy. Cited record.

J27 · Core. A Cookbook for Using the Model-View-Controller User Interface Paradigm in Smalltalk-80 (Krasner et al. (1988)). MVC makes model, view and interaction distinct. A direct historical link cited by Jelly. Cited record.

J28 · Infrastructure. Retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-intensive nlp tasks (Lewis et al. (2020)). Retrieval-augmented generation explains one way to supply information, not who owns a data model. Cited record.

J29 · Core. PUMICE: A Multi-Modal Agent that Learns Concepts and Conditionals from Natural Language and Demonstrations (Li et al. (2019)). PUMICE uses demonstrations and language to teach reusable behavior before the current LLM wave. Cited record.

J30 · Core. End-user programming of mashups with vegemite (Lin et al. (2009)). Vegemite combines web tables and demonstrations to construct small, task-specific automations. Cited record.

J31 · Context. Context-aware online adaptation of mixed reality interfaces (Lindlbauer et al. (2019)). A mixed-reality interface can adapt to context without giving its user a new rule language. Cited record.

J32 · Core. Wildcard: spreadsheet-driven customization of web applications (Litt and Jackson (2020)). Wildcard exposes website data through a table; compare its adapter with Jelly’s generated model. Cited record.

J33 · Context. Design Guidelines for Prompt Engineering Text-to-Image Generative Models (Liu and Chilton (2022)). Prompt-design work in image generation; adjacent evidence about communicating intent. Cited record.

J34 · Method. Management of interface design in HUMANOID (Luo et al. (1993)). HUMANOID separates design concerns to support interface design; read alongside its 1992 account. Cited record.

J35 · Core. Malleable Overview-Detail Interfaces (Min et al. (2025)). A user can change what the overview and detail show; the design problem later addressed by Meridian. Cited record.

J36 · Method. Past, present, and future of user interface software tools (Myers et al. (2000)). Historical synthesis of interface-authoring tools; use for vocabulary and earlier branches. Cited record.

J37 · Method. User interface software tools (Myers (1995a)). Myers’s UI-tools survey; first of two records for the same 1995 article in Jelly. Cited record.

J38 · Duplicate. User interface software tools (Myers (1995b)). Same Myers 1995 article as J37; one work, not two independent pieces of evidence. Cited record.

J39 · Method. Survey on user interface programming (Myers and Rosson (1992)). Survey of programming work on user interfaces; context for the engineering cost of screens. Cited record.

J40 · Core. A small matter of programming: perspectives on end user computing (Nardi (1993)). Nardi’s book explains end-user computing as situated human activity, not simply an easier language. Cited record.

J41 · Core. NL4DV: A toolkit for generating analytic specifications for data visualization from natural language queries (Narechania et al. (2020)). NL4DV turns requests into visualization specifications; an intermediate model makes generation tractable. Cited record.

J42 · Core. The heart of connection: hypermedia unified by transclusion (Nelson (1995)). Transclusion means including by reference; helpful for understanding what a live embed can reuse. Cited record.

J43 · Core. Generating remote control interfaces for complex appliances (Nichols et al. (2002)). A functional appliance description can generate a remote; the controlled object differs from its controls. Cited record.

J44 · Method. Improving automatic interface generation with smart templates (Nichols et al. (2004)). Smart templates encode conventions into generated remote controls. Cited record.

J45 · Method. UNIFORM: automatically generating consistent remote control user interfaces (Nichols et al. (2006a)). UNIFORM investigates consistency among generated remote controls. Cited record.

J46 · Core. Huddle: automatically generating interfaces for systems of multiple connected appliances (Nichols et al. (2006b)). Huddle brings different connected devices into a shared control surface instead of copying each full interface. Cited record.

J47 · Method. User interface management systems: models and algorithms (Olsen (1992)). Reference on models and algorithms for managing interfaces; relevant to runtime foundations. Cited record.

J48 · Method. MIKE: The menu interaction kontrol environment (Olsen Jr (1986)). MIKE is an early interface management environment, long before language-model generation. Cited record.

J49 · Product. Announcing v0: Generative UI (Palmer (2023)). Vercel’s generative UI announcement provides a commercial comparison, not an independent user study. Cited record.

J50 · Core. Towards a general computational framework for model-based interface development systems (Puerta and Eisenstein (1998)). A framework for model-based interface development; identifies where specification and mapping are separate. Jelly lists 1998; the author copy is marked IUI 1999. Cited record.

J51 · Core. Scratch: Programming for All (Resnick et al. (2009)). Scratch lets people compose programs from blocks, including beginners who are not writing textual syntax. Cited record.

J52 · Context. What is it like to program with artificial intelligence? (Sarkar et al. (2022)). Studies the experience of AI-assisted programming rather than evaluating authority after installation. Cited record.

J53 · Core. Vega-lite: A grammar of interactive graphics (Satyanarayan et al. (2016)). Vega-Lite’s grammar makes visual changes expressible as concise specifications. Cited record.

J54 · Infrastructure. Semantic Scholar Academic Graph API (Scholar (nd)). Bibliographic data API: an example of an external source, not a general permission model. Cited record.

J55 · Method. Specification and generation of user interfaces with the boss-system (Schreiber (1994)). BOSS explores interface specification and generation; part of the pre-LLM design family. Cited record.

J56 · Core. Embark: Dynamic Documents as Personal Software (Sonnentag et al. (2023)). Embark uses structured mentions and embedded views in a dynamic document. Cited record.

J57 · Method. Retrospective and challenges for model-based interface development (Szekely (1996)). Retrospective on strengths and difficulties of model-based design. The difficulties also matter for Jelly. Cited record.

J58 · Method. Facilitating the exploration of interface design alternatives: The HUMANOID model of interface design (Szekely et al. (1992)). HUMANOID’s earlier account stresses exploring alternative interface designs. Cited record.

J59 · Method. Declarative interface models for user interface construction tools: The Mastermind approach (Szekely et al. (1996)). Declarative construction models supply a vocabulary for producing interfaces from representations. Cited record.

J60 · Method. A pattern language for human-computer interface design (Tidwell (1997)). Reusable interface design patterns inform decisions about rendering and interaction. Cited record.

J61 · Infrastructure. TripAdvisor Content API (TripAdvisor (nd)). A place/content API supplies information subject to its own terms and access boundary. Cited record.

J62 · Context. Appworld: A controllable world of apps and people for benchmarking interactive coding agents (Trivedi et al. (2024)). AppWorld evaluates agents in controlled app environments; testing tool use is not testing malleability itself. Cited record.

J63 · Core. DynaVis: Dynamically Synthesized UI Widgets for Visualization Editing (Vaithilingam et al. (2024)). DynaVis produces a persistent editing widget from a request; useful contrast with repeatedly prompting. Cited record.

J64 · Core. Bespoke: Interactively Synthesizing Custom GUIs from Command-Line Applications By Demonstration (Vaithilingam and Guo (2019)). Bespoke synthesizes graphical controls from demonstrations of command-line operations. Cited record.

J65 · Method. Knowledge-based systems for automated user interface generation: the trident experience (Vanderdonckt (1995)). TRIDENT is part of the knowledge-based UI-generation lineage. Cited record.

J66 · Core. DynamicLand (Victor (2020)). Dynamicland is a shared physical computing environment. The cited project page is not its invention date. Cited record.

J67 · Method. ITS: A tool for rapidly developing interactive applications (Wiecha et al. (1990)). ITS separates application behavior and its presentation to facilitate interface development. Cited record.

J68 · Core. Ability-based design: Concept, principles and examples (Wobbrock et al. (2011)). Ability-based design treats people’s abilities as design inputs instead of requiring everyone to adapt. Cited record.

J69 · Method. UICoder: Finetuning Large Language Models to Generate User Interface Code through Automated Feedback (Wu et al. (2024)). UICoder improves generated UI code using automatic feedback; compilation is not proof of user control. Cited record.

J70 · Core. Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts (Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. (2023)). Research with non-experts qualifies claims that simply adding a prompt box makes authorship easy. Cited record.

J71 · Method. The auckland layout editor: An improved gui layout specification process (Zeidler et al. (2013)). Auckland Layout Editor exposes layout specification; concerns geometry more than authority or data ownership. Cited record.

J72 · Context. How do Data Science Workers Collaborate? Roles, Workflows, and Tools (Zhang et al. (2020)). Observations of data-science collaboration supply background about actual multi-person workflows. Cited record.

J73 · Infrastructure. Adding conditional control to text-to-image diffusion models (Zhang et al. (2023)). Conditioning image generation is a related generative technique, not an end-user software system. Cited record.

J74 · Method. Screen Recognition: Creating Accessibility Metadata for Mobile Applications from Pixels (Zhang et al. (2021)). Recovering semantic screen structure can improve accessibility; appearance alone omits useful information. Cited record.

J75 · Core. Fusion: Opportunistic Web Prototyping with UI Mashups (Zhang and Guo (2018)). Fusion composes pieces of existing web UIs; compare reuse of visible parts with reuse of structured data. Cited record.

The Ink and Switch reading trail

The essay uses inline hyperlinks rather than a numbered bibliography. Below are its 55 distinct linked reading or example destinations in order of first appearance in the essay body, including historical and commercial illustrations. Internal navigation, repeated identical links, credits, and the newsletter signup are excluded. An essay and a gallery inside it may be separate link destinations but are not two papers. Where an original link is general-interest coverage, consult the scholarly companion listed beside it for technical claims.

I01. How Buildings Learn. Analogy: occupants keep adapting a building after its designers leave.

I02. Why Doctors Hate Their Computers. First-person reporting about software that can dictate working practices.

I03. Designing and Programming Malleable Software. Dissertation and Tangler: a direct scholarly predecessor. N18.

I04. Webstrates project. An editable shared substrate; see also the paper R17.

I05. Computer Software. Kay’s 1984 article, distinct from his word processor article. R09.

I06. Video game modding. Illustration of after-market changes, not a study of all games.

I07. Unsanity and Mac system modifications. Historical example of extending systems without a stable official interface.

I08. Prefab. Research paper using pixel-based inference to support new behavior. J12.

I09. Adversarial interoperability. EFF essay on making systems work together without the incumbent’s cooperation.

I10. School lunch generator. Newspaper account of a personal application; anecdotal evidence.

I11. Reforestation tracker. Newspaper account of building a specific tool rather than a general study.

I12. Japanese translation tool. Litt’s personal account of rapid LLM-assisted development. N24.

I13. Malleable Systems Collective catalog. Discovery directory, not a single research result. N34.

I14. User-tailorable systems and Buttons. The customization learning slope and sharing changes. R12.

I15. Opening the Hood of a Word Processor. Kay’s separate 1984 article. N08.

I16. End-user Programming. Ink & Switch’s earlier lab essay about editing in place. N19.

I17. Stylish and user styles. Changing a page’s presentation through reusable styles.

I18. Arc Boosts. A browser feature for customization. Read as a historical example; current support may differ.

I19. Macro systems reading. The original essay’s linked record on automating repeated actions.

I20. Tampermonkey. A userscript manager; scripts can extend page behavior within a browser.

I21. AppleScript Language Guide. Vendor documentation for automation expressed in a scripting language.

I22. LIVE programming community. Venue and further prototypes for programming with live feedback.

I23. Excel Flash Fill. Vendor documentation about learning transformations from examples.

I24. Hedy. Gradual programming language as a way to introduce more expressive constructs.

I25. Instrumental Interaction. Disentangling an interaction instrument from the object it operates on. N14.

I26. A World Without Apps. Talk; a vision of computing in terms other than sealed applications.

I27. Smalltalk. Overview link in the essay; use R07 and N06 for first-hand technical accounts.

I28. OpenDoc Programmer’s Guide. Programmer documentation on compound documents and editable parts.

I29. Object Linking and Embedding. Background link; use R61 for vendor documentation.

I30. Varv. A declarative representation for extending interactive behavior. R27.

I31. Dynamicland. Official site for the communal computing research environment. R19.

I32. Boxer. Official project and archived literature on a reconstructible medium. R10.

I33. Webstrates paper. The peer-reviewed basis for the shared-media discussion. R17.

I34. Substrates 2025 workshop. Contemporary venue for work on new computational media. N37.

I35. The inequities of our remote gathering tools. A practitioner account of how a group is constrained by fixed tools.

I36. Twinkling lights and nested loops. Field research on cooperation around spreadsheets. N12.

I37. Situated Software. Shirky’s essay about software made for specific social situations. N15.

I38. An app can be a home-cooked meal. Sloan’s first-person account of building for a very small audience. N20.

I39. Run your own social. Community-scale operation and adaptation of social infrastructure.

I40. Local-first software. Local copies and long-term user control as architectural goals. R20.

I41. Automerge. Maintained synchronization technology, not a guarantee of correct permissions. R58.

I42. PushPin. Peer-to-peer collaboration and composable material on a board. R24.

I43. Cambria. Schema translation between old and new tools. R21.

I44. Farm. Experimental environment and repository. R59.

I45. Universal Version Control. Research program on histories beyond source code. N35.

I46. Bootstrapping Research. Dynamicland talk about supporting research with one’s own tools.

I47. Artifacts. Vendor documentation; a generated artifact is not automatically integrated with another product.

I48. Patchwork notebook on comments. Lab example of supporting a reusable commenting tool.

I49. Patchwork lab notebook. Dated record of experiments, not one final universal product.

I50. Potluck. Adding computation to a freeform note. R25.

I51. Potluck gallery. Examples inside the same Potluck report, not a second paper.

I52. AI and Potluck demonstration. Follow-on video linked by the later essay; distinguish it from the original report.

I53. Embark. Places, dates, formulas and views sharing the context of an outline. R35.

I54. Programmable Ink. Umbrella program; see Inkbase and Untangle for particular prototypes.

I55. Inverting three key relationships. Related practitioner essay linked from the discussion of new computing environments.
